title: Written down
hook: in the first century BCE the Pali canon was written on palm leaves at Aluvihara

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sanghamitta, a branch in a golden vessel and a king wading into the sea. Your line: it still grows.

A strip of dried palm leaf, long and narrow, lies across a monk's knee. He scratches letters into it with a metal stylus, line after careful line. Later, soot and oil are rubbed across the leaf and wiped away, and the dark stays only in the scratches, so the words appear. A whole library can be made this way, one leaf at a time, tied between wooden boards. In Sri Lanka, the chronicle says, there came a day when the monks decided the teaching had to be written down in books.
screen: `A STRIP OF PALM LEAF.` → `A STYLUS SCRATCHES LETTERS.` → `THE MONKS DECIDE.`

segments.voice: First, a teaching that lived in voices. Monks learned the discourses and the rules by heart and chanted them together, so one person's mistake could be caught by the others. The chronicles of Sri Lanka say the three baskets of the teaching, and the commentaries on them, had been handed down that way, by mouth. Second, the fear. The Mahavamsa sets this moment in the reign of King Vattagamani, a troubled reign in which the king himself is driven from his throne for a time. The monks saw that people were falling away, the chronicle says, so they came together and wrote the texts down in books, that the true teaching might endure. That's the whole reason it gives. Not convenience. Survival. Third, the place. Tradition names it as Aluvihara, a monastery among great rocks, and pilgrims still visit. Fourth, what changed and what didn't. Writing didn't end the chanting. Monks still learn texts by heart and recite them together, and in monasteries today the voice is still one way the teaching is received. But now there was a second, quieter keeper: leaves in a bundle, waiting for anyone who could read. When a manuscript wore out, it could be copied fresh. That's how a text stays alive, the way a tree does: not by never changing, but by being renewed. The monks at Aluvihara didn't know who would read their leaves. They wrote for strangers, so the teaching wouldn't depend on any one memory, or any one life.
screen: `A TEACHING THAT LIVED IN VOICES.` · `AFRAID IT COULD BE LOST.` · `WRITTEN AT ALUVIHARA.` · `CHANTING GOES ON.`

segments.voice: With paper and a pen, or a note on your phone, choose one line that matters to you, from these lessons, from someone you love, or from a text of your own tradition. Write it slowly, letter by letter, the way the monk scratched each letter into the leaf, then read it back once and let it rest with you while you breathe.
Written down. The moment, as the chronicle tells it, when the teaching carried by voices was set down in books, so it would endure.
Your line: on palm leaves. They wrote for readers they would never meet. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada monasteries keep both ways alive: monks memorize and chant the texts together, and the written canon, once kept on palm leaves, is now printed and studied as well.

original.note: Pali: pitaka, a basket. the canon is called the three baskets.

trapdoor: what you thought: someone sat down one day and wrote the Buddhist bible.
what it means: in the chronicle, texts long kept by memory were written in books, so they wouldn't be lost in hard times.
what a scholar hears: the Mahavamsa gives the reason in a few lines and sets it in Vattagamani's reign; the name Aluvihara comes from tradition, and chanting carried on beside the written page.

chat.says: Why did monks write the teaching down if they'd memorized it?
options: The chronicle says they feared it could be lost in troubled times.
Writing was easier, so they stopped chanting the texts altogether.
A king ordered it, so that he could keep the only copy himself.
chat.meaning: In the Mahavamsa, in Vattagamani's troubled reign, monks saw people falling away and wrote the texts in books so the teaching would endure.

Vattagamani.meaning: the king whose troubled reign saw the texts written down

Aluvihara.meaning: a rock monastery where tradition says the texts were written

Mahavamsa.meaning: a chronicle of Sri Lanka's Buddhist history

stylus.meaning: a pointed metal tool for scratching letters

sources.ref: Mahavamsa 33 (the reign of Vattagamani; the texts written in books)

notes: The outline hook gives 'the first century BCE'; the chronicle names the reign, not a century, so the script leaves the date out (claims rule). A Keeper may want the scholarly dating added with attribution.
